newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu strained by cabinet squabbles.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu strained by cabinet squabbles.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu struggled on Sunday to quench wildfires in his tumultuous cabinet ahead of a government shake-up expected this week.

Netanyahu met Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon, an ultra-hawk tipped to be named finance minister who demands a central role in Arab-Israeli peacemaking, in the wake of a disclosure Sharon held secret talks with a Palestinian leader close to President Yasser Arafat.

Foreign Minister David Levy, deeply entrenched in a power struggle with Netanyahu over peacemaking responsibilities, cancelled a conciliatory meeting with the prime minister after learning of Sharon's secret meeting through the media.

"The prime minister and minister Sharon held consultations between them. The prime minister intends to continue his series of meetings tomorrow with the foreign minister, defence minister and other ministers," Netanyahu's spokesman said in a statement.
The statement said Netanyahu would announce his cabinet decisions after completing the negotiations. "No meetings with ministers have been set at this stage," it added.

Israel Channel One broadcast news over the weekend that the burly Sharon, a champion of Jewish settlement in occupied Arab lands, had this month met Mahmoud Abbas, a PLO architect of peace moves better known as Abu Mazen.
Ex-general Sharon, 69, has been a recalcitrant cabinet opponent of peacemaking with the PLO, branding Arafat a "war criminal". Sharon's right-wing allies said they were "stunned" by the meeting.
"It certainly is worrisome," Transport Minister Yitzhak Levy of the National Religious Party told Israeli army radio. "My worry is where is Sharon situated from a political standpoint."
Other Israelis speculated that Sharon aimed to soften his hardline image before assuming his highest job in government since a 1982 massacre of Palestinians forced his ouster as defence minister.

"That's the $64,000 question," said political analyst Hanan Crystal when asked whether Sharon was a reborn pragmatist or merely a shrewd tactician trying to win a seat on Netanyahu's three-man "kitchen cabinet" which oversees Israeli peace moves.
Political sources say Levy and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai both oppose giving Sharon a place on the inner team.

Netanyahu, 47, has lurched from crisis to crisis since he took power a year ago. His cabinet is in turmoil and peacemaking has crumbled over his expansion of Jewish settlements in the West Bank and Gaza.

Sharon and Abu Mazen both refrained from commenting but Israeli and Palestinian officials confirmed the meeting. At his Gaza headquarters Arafat said the meeting, aimed at reviving peace moves, was coordinated with him.

Yossi Beilin, a leader of the opposition Labour party which launched peace moves with the PLO, said: "It proves again that if in the Israel of 1997 you want to be part of the foreign and security policy establishment, you must meet PLO people.

"The meeting and I imagine the timing of the leak were meant to show the world that look, 'I am not so extreme, I can speak with them'," Beilin told Israel Radio. But he doubted Sharon or Netanyahu could break out of the crisis in peacemaking.

"I certainly see Sharon continuing to be a problem both from a symbolic standpoint and a standpoint of substance. His programme cannot be accepted by anyone. Maybe in Israel there are some who would accept it, but certainly not in the world."

In 1983 a state inquiry forced Sharon out as defence minister after finding him indirectly responsible for the massacre of hundreds of Palestinians at two refugee camps near Beirut by Israeli-backed Christian militiamen.
